video_title: Will Every Failed Crypto Idea Work? - The Chopping Block
gist: The Chopping Block panel (Dragonfly host, Tom, Tarun of Gauntlet) plus Y Combinator's Neil debate Imran of Alliance DAO's claim that almost every failed crypto idea (NFTs, creator tokens, DAOs, gaming, TCRs, onchain reputation, rebase tokens, decentralized storage) will eventually work, against a backdrop of BitMEX, BitMart, Movement Labs, Storj Labs and Balancer Labs winding down. The host argues crypto is a finance-only technology and that ideas not born from a demand signal are self-delusion, while Neil counters that 'money is everything' and that YC's 'why now' test is what separates Webvan from Instacart. The back half turns to AI x crypto: agent payments, Cloudflare pay-per-crawl, the collapse of the ad-funded internet, and whether AI capex can ever be covered by ads.

themes.theme: 2026 crypto shakeout: exchanges and labs winding down

insights.claim: BitMEX, the exchange that invented the perpetual swap, is shutting down on September 23rd after 11 years, having fallen from the number one crypto derivatives venue to an also-ran as compliance costs rose and trading volume fell.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: The venue that seeded the derivatives industry dying while perps become a mainstream product shows value accrues to distribution and compliance, not to the original innovator — watch for further consolidation of derivatives volume into licensed incumbents.

insights.claim: Alongside BitMEX, exchange BitMart plus protocol-side companies Storj Labs, Movement Labs and Balancer Labs are all winding down, and the panel notes each shutdown now generates less surprise than the last.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Onchain project entities are now actually dying rather than zombie-shuffling, so token holders can no longer assume a permanent floor from 'someone will always run a node'.

insights.claim: The old crypto assumption that protocols and tokens never truly go to zero has broken — things are now genuinely going to zero.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Repricing long-tail tokens for real terminal risk rather than perpetual optionality changes how a crypto portfolio should be sized and hedged.
insights.quote: So like nothing ever goes to zero, but things are actually going to zero now.

insights.claim: Neil of Y Combinator says he has never been more bullish despite the wave of shutdowns, because BitMEX's core innovation was absorbed by the rest of the market — Coinbase is launching perps in the US and Binance has run them for years.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: The diffusion of perps into regulated venues means derivatives revenue is migrating to listed and institutional platforms rather than disappearing.
insights.quote: I would say like despite all those shutdowns, I've never been more bullish.

insights.claim: Coinbase's 'everything exchange' strategy is an explicit acknowledgement that a pure-crypto venue is not viable and that prediction markets and equities must sit alongside crypto, while every major US and global financial institution adds crypto trading from the other direction.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: The line between crypto exchanges and brokerages is dissolving, so competitive analysis for Coinbase should be run against retail brokers and prediction-market venues, not just crypto exchanges.

insights.claim: The rise of the 'labs plus governance token' structure was largely a function of the absence of US regulatory clarity, and clarity is arriving even before the Clarity Act passes — evidenced by Hester Pierce's recent post signalling the government wants to get out of the way.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: If the labs/governance-token wrapper was a regulatory artifact, expect new projects to default to conventional corporate structures and equity, reducing future token supply from infrastructure teams.

themes.theme: The 'every failed idea will work' debate and the why-now test

insights.claim: Imran of Alliance DAO's viral tweet claims almost everything in crypto that failed the first time will eventually work, naming NFTs, creator tokens, DAOs, gaming, TCRs, onchain reputation, rebase tokens and decentralized storage — and the Dragonfly host publicly attacked it as toxic positivity that discourages studying the idea maze.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: The framing sets the bar for evaluating any 'this failed idea is back' pitch: demand for a specific artifact-level revival should be treated as a red flag absent an environmental change.
insights.quote: I think this is a toxic attitude to take.

insights.claim: The strongest counterexamples to the failed-ideas-stay-dead view are Polymarket and Hyperliquid — ideas that did not work for a very long time and then started working.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Both revivals happened in financial verticals with real demand signals, which is a screen for which dormant categories are worth re-underwriting.

insights.claim: Y Combinator's core screening question in its 10-minute founder interviews is the 'why now' — what changed in the world that makes an idea that was terrible a few years ago viable, and how the founder's approach differs from predecessors'.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: A reusable diligence filter: reject revival pitches that cannot name a specific substrate change (regulation, install base, liquidity, UX, AI agents) rather than just asserting inevitability.

insights.claim: Neil's Webvan-versus-Instacart comparison is that Instacart succeeded because mobile phones existed and because it hired shoppers to buy from existing stores rather than building capex-heavy fulfilment on day one — the same lean, no-new-infrastructure pattern crypto founders should copy.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Prefer crypto teams that compose existing rails and APIs over teams that must first build a chain or network before delivering the product.

insights.claim: Marc Andreessen's observation that literally every idea pitched during the dotcom bubble eventually came true is the strongest case for the revival thesis, but timing is what determines investment outcomes.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Being directionally right on a category is worthless without timing the substrate change — argues for buying revivals only after a demand signal is visible, not on narrative.
insights.quote: every idea that we were pitched during the dotcom bubble eventually came true. Literally, every single one.

insights.claim: The host will only believe NFTs come back if the world moves into pervasive VR — he can construct that 2035 scenario, but cannot even imagine what would have to change for creator tokens or crypto gaming, which he now thinks are simply incorrect mappings of incentives.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Distinguishes 'blocked on a missing substrate' categories (potentially investable later) from 'structurally wrong' ones (never), which is how to triage dormant crypto sectors.

insights.claim: Tom argues path dependency and founder effects determine outcomes for identical ideas, citing DoorDash winning by seeding suburban chain restaurants while Postmates and GrubHub fought over cities, and Reddit versus Digg being near-identical products with different seed communities.
insights.speaker: Tom
insights.so_what: A failed crypto category may deserve a second look purely on a different go-to-market or seed community, independent of any technology change.

insights.claim: Tarun argues most 2013-2017 crypto designs embedded a hidden homo economicus assumption — a perfectly rational participant who would reallocate all resources to whichever network had the best white paper — and that when enough participants do not care, systems like DAO governance and TCRs become easy to manipulate.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Mechanism designs that rely on broad attentive participation should be underwritten as manipulable by default; only designs robust to apathy are investable.
insights.quote: my network had the best white paper

insights.claim: The host's central thesis is that unlike the internet, crypto is not an everything technology but a 'many things' technology and plausibly an everything-financial technology — the further an idea sits from money, contracts and assets, the less it has been vindicated.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Argues for concentrating crypto exposure in financial primitives (stablecoins, perps, prediction markets, RWA) and treating non-financial verticals as structurally uninvestable.
insights.quote: I think crypto is not an everything technology I think it is many things technology. I think it is plausibly in everything financial technology.

insights.claim: Base publicly conceded its consumer-social bet was wrong for now: Jesse's long post admitted the creator-token and Zora-adjacent social push distracted Base and left it behind on real-world assets, tokenization and prediction markets, and he handed the Base app to Kobe while refocusing himself on the Base chain.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: The largest well-funded test of consumer crypto social publicly capitulating toward financial use cases is a strong signal on where L2 ecosystem funding and attention flow next.
insights.quote: I I I don't believe that we're wrong forever, but we're definitely wrong for right now.

insights.claim: Neil pushes back that money is bigger than the panel assumes — even decentralized storage is fundamentally an allocation-of-resources-at-a-price problem, which is why Filecoin chose a blockchain — and that the blockchain's real superpower is capital formation, something every company on earth needs.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Reframes 'crypto is only finance' as bullish rather than limiting, and points capital toward primary-issuance and capital-formation rails as the durable category.
insights.quote: I think the blockchain is the greatest capital innovation machine in the world

insights.claim: The host's test for whether a category will eventually work is whether everyone already knows what the killer product feels like — true for AI, VR and stablecoins, and not true for decentralized social, where nobody can articulate why the decentralized version would beat centralized alternatives.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: A cheap screen for narrative categories: if you cannot describe the finished product's appeal in one sentence to a non-user, the demand may not exist at all.
insights.quote: If you 10 years ago, if I told you you can send dollars anywhere instantaneously 24/7 to anyone with a mobile phone, will that have product market fit? If you can do it, yes.

insights.claim: Blockchain is a mechanism rather than a thesis, and 'X on the blockchain' pitches fail because the underlying business is usually not the two-sided marketplace it appears to be — Airbnb and Uber are trust, curation, fraud and operations businesses, exactly where blockchains are disadvantaged.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Kills a whole class of pitches on structure alone and identifies trust/curation/fraud as the diligence question for any marketplace-on-chain proposal.
insights.quote: It's a trust business, a curation business, a fraud business. And blockchains suck at that stuff.

insights.claim: The host's heuristic for avoiding hyped crypto dead ends is to follow demand signals, because nearly every idea on the failed list originated from investors and founders blog-posting each other into consensus rather than from observed user demand.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Directly usable allocation filter — demand-signal origin versus thesis-origin explains much of the last cycle's dispersion in crypto venture returns.
insights.quote: if you're not starting from a demand signal, you are probably fooling yourself

themes.theme: YC founder counsel: tokens late, pain points first

insights.claim: At YC's Startup School at the Chase Center with roughly 7,000 builders, almost no one raised their hand when asked if they were launching a token early — a marked shift from the top of the last crypto bull market.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: New-issuance supply from the current founder cohort should be materially lower, which matters for the token supply overhang that weighed on the last cycle.
insights.quote: almost no one raised their hand

insights.claim: Neil counsels founders against launching a token early because gating product access behind a token shrinks the addressable market, and because free money attracts users who reveal nothing about genuine product demand.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Incentivized usage metrics should be discounted entirely in diligence; the same logic implies post-incentive retention is the only real PMF read on token-subsidized protocols.
insights.quote: I suddenly think your TAM, your addressable market goes down a lot.

insights.claim: Neil's diagnosis of failed crypto products is that teams solve their own problem rather than the customer's, and that an early token warps founder vision because rising prices make any product look like it has demand.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Explains why product signal from bull-market cohorts is unreliable, and why bear-market cohorts are a cleaner read on durable demand.
insights.quote: we sometimes try to solve things that are our problem, but not our customer's problem

insights.claim: Neil argues decentralization maximalism is the biggest handicap of crypto-native founders because users do not care about decentralization, and points to stablecoins as the proof — centralized products running on decentralized infrastructure that solve an obvious pain point.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Supports underwriting centralized issuers and app-layer businesses on public chains rather than paying a premium for decentralization purity.
insights.quote: users don't care about decentralization

insights.claim: Neil proposes that crypto capital formation needs a standardization moment analogous to YC's SAFE — which replaced $30,000-$60,000 bespoke rounds full of founder-hostile terms — to keep blockchain's fundraising power while removing early exit liquidity and over-funding of the wrong protocols.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: A standard token-raise instrument would be a genuine structural change for primary crypto markets — worth watching who ships one.

themes.theme: Stablecoin infrastructure and the hidden institutional demand

insights.claim: YC currently has four or five stablecoin infrastructure companies that almost nobody has heard of, including Infinia and Blind Pay, because they sell to developers and businesses rather than building consumer brands.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: The growth layer of crypto is B2B stablecoin plumbing, which is invisible in consumer app metrics and token prices — a sourcing area rather than a trade.

insights.claim: Payroll providers Gusto and Deel are running payroll on stablecoins and need underlying infrastructure to do it, exemplifying a shift from consumer-facing crypto to selling into banks and fintechs behind the scenes.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Stablecoin volume growth is increasingly embedded in non-crypto SaaS workflows, so payments-infrastructure revenue can grow while crypto asset prices stagnate.

insights.claim: Neil says not a week passes without a bank or institutional investment firm somewhere in the world approaching him to integrate crypto, usually in ways hidden from the end user — the opposite of the older assumption that everyone would consciously interact with wallets.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: If adoption is invisible and intermediated, consumer wallet metrics understate real usage and the value may accrue to embedded infrastructure providers rather than consumer brands.
insights.quote: I don't think a week passes without a financial institution reaching out to me, a bank or institutional investment firm somewhere in the world that's excited to integrate crypto in some way.

insights.claim: Neil finds it disappointing that most current crypto building is a direct analog of existing TradFi products, comparing it to using the internet only for newspapers rather than inventing something structurally new like Facebook.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Implies the largest future returns sit in a native, not-yet-invented category, so an all-in RWA/stablecoin allocation may be underwriting the low-multiple part of the opportunity.
insights.quote: that's like saying that the internet was great for newspapers

themes.theme: DAOs, onchain reputation and onchain credit

insights.claim: The host argues the historical record shows DAOs are reliably worse than almost any other form of corporate governance and that the failure is a deep structural property, not a tooling or membership-quality problem.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: A hard prior against protocols choosing DAO governance and a reason to prefer protocols that have re-centralized decision-making into companies or foundations.
insights.quote: it's very obvious from the record that if you can avoid being a Dow, you should. You will be better at doing your job if you're not a DAO.

insights.claim: Purely onchain credit fails because addresses are repudiable — a borrower can default and abandon the address — and because there is no recourse mechanism such as a lien or wage garnishment, which is why every working onchain credit business reaches offchain into KYC and real-business underwriting.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Any onchain lending pitch should be evaluated on its offchain enforcement stack, not its smart contracts — the credit risk lives entirely there.

insights.claim: Tom argues onchain reputation and proof of humanity are newly interesting because online personas, content and claims have increased by orders of magnitude, and order-of-magnitude changes usually mean prior approaches must be redesigned.
insights.speaker: Tom
insights.so_what: AI-driven fake-persona inflation is the concrete 'why now' for identity and reputation infrastructure — the category most likely to be revived from the failed list.

insights.claim: The host revives the Debt DAO concept as newly plausible for a cash-generating protocol like Hyperliquid — protocol-level debt where holders are contractually paid from revenues before equity-like token distributions, enforced by smart contracts rather than courts.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Protocol-level debt against fee revenue would be a genuinely new onchain fixed-income instrument — watch high-revenue protocols for the first issuance.
insights.quote: Maybe Hyperl could take on debt as a protocol and basically like the debt holders are guaranteed to get paid first before equity holders get distributed dividends.

insights.claim: Neil's preferred TCR reboot is data collectives where contributors receive a quasi-equity claim on a data repository over time, and he says the unsolved prize is using tokens to bootstrap two-sided marketplaces without the token turning into a game that later implodes.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Names the specific unsolved mechanism-design problem whose solution would unlock a large category — useful as a thesis to source against.

themes.theme: AI x crypto: agent payments and the broken ad model

insights.claim: Machine-to-machine payments have been proposed repeatedly since Bitcoin mining pools around 2011 and IOTA-style IoT blockchains in 2017, and the panel says it is only now feasible without a leap of faith — Neil notes the machine-payments standard his team shipped at Coinbase (rendered 'X42' in the captions) traces back to a 2011 Bitcointalk post whose why-now is simply that agents exist.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet) and Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Agent payments is the one revived idea the panel broadly agrees has a genuine why-now, making it the highest-priority category from the failed-ideas list.
insights.quote: the why now was basically agents exist now

insights.claim: Cloudflare has announced it will gate websites behind pay-per-crawl using crypto, and Neil is uncertain whether per-crawl micropayments will actually clear or whether Cloudflare simply signs bulk business-development deals with large AI labs instead.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: The single most watchable live experiment for whether crypto micropayments find real agent-driven demand — outcome determines the agent-payments TAM.

insights.claim: The host predicts agent micropayments will re-converge on bundling, subscriptions and intermediaries because per-request payment construction consumes agent tokens — friction does not disappear with agents, it reappears in a different form.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Argues against a pure per-call micropayment future and toward aggregators sitting between agents and content — a different investable layer than the payment rail itself.

insights.claim: Tarun argues agents should be treated as a magic alien with capabilities humans lack — they may prefer bundling millions of transactions at once — rather than being given human-speed peer-to-peer payment patterns.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Suggests the winning agent-payment design is unlike any existing human payment product, so incumbency in consumer payments may not transfer.
insights.quote: We should treat them as this like magic alien that can do something you can't do.

insights.claim: Tarun maps the AI stack onto crypto market structure: AI frontends and harnesses are wallets, routers are DEX aggregators and bridges, models are protocols that cannot extract much fee, and inference providers are liquidity providers earning yield on deployed capital.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: If the analogy holds, AI value accrues at the edges (interfaces and inference capital) and not to model layers — a direct read on where AI margins should be underwritten.
insights.quote: harnesses like frontends and harnesses for AI are wallets. Routers are like dex aggregators and kind of bridges

insights.claim: Tarun notes Jason Calacanis reversed his 'if you're in crypto, pivot to AI' position to 'if you're in crypto use AI' after a long Brian Armstrong tweet, and argues today's mid-tier AI labs have white-paper energy — US open-source labs are largely white papers while the Chinese labs have delivered, the inverse of the 2017 US-versus-Chinese L1 dynamic.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: A skeptical frame for US open-model announcements: judge on shipped weights and usage, not benchmark claims, exactly as with 2017 chain TPS numbers.
insights.quote: the Chinese ones are the only ones who've delivered

insights.claim: Tom draws a licensing parallel between crypto's use of BSL and the new AI weight licenses — the Kimi weights are viewable and usable but require a paid license to sell inference, mirroring MongoDB-style source-available terms.
insights.speaker: Tom
insights.so_what: Source-available licensing is becoming the monetization template for both crypto protocols and open-weight models, which changes how forkability risk should be priced.

insights.claim: Neil argues AI is destroying the internet's ad-based monetization model because the agent, not the publisher, will serve and capture ad revenue, leaving unresolved how any of it gets distributed back to smaller content providers.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: A structural short on the long tail of ad-funded publishing and a demand source for new content-monetization rails.
insights.quote: we basically destroy the monetization model of the internet uh right now because ads essentially are going to are not going to work in the way that they are today

insights.claim: AI labs are already paying bulk rates of $10 million to $20 million to scrape sources like the New York Times, which Neil expects to leave smaller providers needing a shared subscription or billing collective that he hopes is decentralized rather than controlled by one company.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Bulk licensing already clears at the top; the unserved long tail is the addressable market for a crypto-native content-payments layer.
insights.quote: the labs are already paying bulk rate to like scrape the New York Times. They're paying $10 million or $20 million.

insights.claim: Tarun's crude but forceful argument that ads cannot fund AI is that the highest free-cash-flow businesses in the world have gone cash-flow negative within one year on capex, a capex-to-cash-flow relationship he says has no precedent since the World War II era.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: If advertising cannot cover AI capex, either new monetization (transaction take rates) emerges or the capex cycle reprices — the central risk for big-tech multiples.
insights.quote: look at the capex relative to free cash flow. It's like I don't think you've seen anything like this since the like World War II era.

insights.claim: Tarun argues the open-source economics of the Linux era — expensive creation followed by zero marginal cost forever — do not hold for AI, where open weights still carry a high and permanent inference marginal cost, breaking the pure subsidy model.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Open-weight releases are not commoditizing AI the way open source commoditized software, so inference capacity and cost curves remain the durable moat to track.
insights.quote: now it's like actually the marginal cost is quite high forever

insights.claim: Neil counters that AI monetization solves itself through falling cost curves plus outcome-based pricing — taking roughly 2% of a purchase the agent facilitated — which the panel maps to payment for order flow accruing at the interface and inference edges.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: If agent commerce take rates replace ads, the winners are whoever owns the agent interface — the same position wallets hold in crypto.
insights.quote: it's like I'm going to take 2% of your order because I help like support it and set it up

insights.claim: Neil argues the AI agent becomes the new browser and the gateway to everything, with every user interface rethought to route through it, giving whoever owns that layer enormous market power — and cites Sam Altman describing OpenAI's new phase as utility, implying massive scale at low margins.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: A utility-margin AI layer with gateway control implies value capture shifts to distribution and transaction take rates rather than model licensing.
insights.quote: the new phase of open AI is utility

themes.theme: Centralization gravity and the innovation cycle

insights.claim: The host's biggest belief change since 2020 is the inversion of the inevitability thesis: technologies do not naturally decentralize, they push toward intermediation, aggregation and bundling, and decentralization only survives where users actively demand it.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Removes the free option from 'decentralization will win eventually' theses and argues for underwriting demand for decentralization explicitly, per market.
insights.quote: things don't want to be decentralized things actually naturally push against decentralization

insights.claim: The host says the default equilibrium in most markets is roughly three exchanges owning most of the market, where being delisted means having no liquidity — not fifty venues with equal share.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Argues for concentrating exposure in top-tier venues and pricing listing access as a real dependency for any token.
insights.quote: it's like three exchanges and they own most of the market and ultimately if you can't if you get kicked off of them, then you have no liquidity

insights.claim: Neil describes himself as an innovation maxi: innovation, not decentralization technology, is what breaks up incumbent centralization — and it simply creates the next generation of centralized winners, as seen in Google going from unassailable to running scared within a decade.
insights.speaker: Neil (Y Combinator, ex-Coinbase)
insights.so_what: Reframes the crypto bet as a bet on the rate of innovation disrupting incumbents rather than on decentralization as an end state — different holdings follow.
insights.quote: I'm actually an innovation maxi which is that if you have new things like blockchains, if you have new things like AI, they actually disrupt the powers that be.
